title: Giving Measurements a Place
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Python can keep values in an ordered list or find them by name in a dictionary. NumPy arrays give numerical data a consistent layout for calculation, so we need to understand what each position represents.

title: Which Direction Are We Adding?
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: Rows and columns give a table different directions. Averaging down a column answers a different question from averaging across a row. NumPy calls these directions axes, and choosing one determines which observations we combine.

title: Preparing the Arrays We Need
topic: From a measurement to a calculation
blurb: We often know the size of an array or the spacing of a sequence before collecting its values. NumPy can create those layouts directly. The initial values need a clear meaning, especially when zero could be mistaken for a measurement.

title: Choose the Readings Without Losing Their Place
blurb: Selecting data means identifying the entries we actually want. Slices select ranges, while explicit indices select particular positions. Some selections share storage with the original array, which matters if we intend to change the result.

title: Put the Same Readings Into the Right Arrangement
blurb: An array's arrangement determines which values a calculation treats together. Reshaping changes that arrangement, while a transpose exchanges its axes. The resulting dimensions need to preserve the meaning of the observations, even when the numbers themselves are unchanged.

title: One Reference for Many Rows
blurb: One reference value, or one row of reference values, often needs to apply across a larger array. NumPy can match those values using the arrays' shapes. We need to check that the matching agrees with what the data represents.

title: Ask Each Row a Question
blurb: A condition can give us a yes-or-no answer for every entry in an array. Those answers form a mask that selects the values we need, while preserving their order and keeping the original data available.

title: Summarize a Report Without Losing the Question
blurb: A summary combines many observations into fewer answers. The largest value and the position where it occurred tell us different things. Choosing the right NumPy operation means keeping that distinction, along with the direction of the calculation.

title: One Calculation for a Whole Report
blurb: Array operations let NumPy perform repeated calculations inside its compiled routines. We can understand them by first following the equivalent steps one value at a time. A shorter expression still needs checking for the temporary arrays and memory it requires.

title: Turn Several Measurements Into Several Predictions
blurb: A prediction can combine several measurements using a coefficient for each one. Matrix multiplication applies that calculation across a table. Understanding how the rows and columns match also helps us solve equations and fit approximate relationships to observations.

title: When Two Calculations Almost Agree
blurb: Computer arithmetic can introduce small rounding differences. We need a reason for the error we allow, and separate checks for a result with the wrong dimensions or missing values. A close-looking answer alone does not establish that the calculation is correct.

title: Can We Repeat the Same Experiment?
blurb: Random selections can change the result of an experiment. Recording how we made those choices lets us repeat a comparison and investigate a change. Repeatability still leaves us with the question of how well that sample represents other observations.

title: Give a Reusable Calculation a Clear Contract
blurb: A function gives a calculation one place to live and makes it reusable with new data. Its inputs need an agreed meaning, and its result needs a clear format. Tests help us check that agreement beyond the first example.

title: Keep Enough of a Calculation to Run It Again
blurb: Saving numerical work means preserving enough information to repeat it. NumPy's array files retain shapes and data types, while text files need more explicit interpretation. Related arrays also need names and an agreed order when we load them again.

title: What Does One Row Actually Describe?
blurb: A table organizes records into rows with named fields. Before querying it, we need to understand what one row describes and which identifier distinguishes it from another. That choice determines how the stored facts can be combined later.

title: Which Columns Answer the Question?
blurb: A query can return only the fields needed for a report, including calculated values with useful names. Removing repeated results requires another decision: which selected fields together define a duplicate? SELECT and DISTINCT make those choices explicit.

title: Which Inspection Records Need Our Attention?
blurb: A database question becomes a condition that each row must satisfy. SQL combines those conditions with AND and OR. Their grouping matters because a small change in the condition can select a different population of records.

title: Which Two Visits Took the Longest?
blurb: A table has no guaranteed reading order. A ranked report needs an explicit sorting rule before selecting its first results, including a decision about tied values. That makes the shortlist reproducible when the database reads the same records differently.

title: Was the Visit Instant, or Is Its Duration Missing?
blurb: A missing measurement tells us something different from a recorded zero. SQL represents missing values with NULL, which can make a comparison unknown. That affects which rows a filter keeps and how we interpret the resulting report.

title: What Should Botie Label Each Reading?
blurb: A report may need a label derived from the values in each row. CASE expresses that decision as ordered conditions. The first true condition determines the result, so missing values and exact thresholds need deliberate treatment.

title: How Much Inspection Time Did We Actually Record?
blurb: A total or average summarizes a collection of rows, but missing values affect what it describes. Counting records differs from counting known measurements. We need to keep that distinction visible when reporting a summary or interpreting an empty result.

title: How Much Work Belongs to Each Asset?
blurb: An overall total can hide how work is distributed. GROUP BY collects rows with the same key and calculates a summary within each collection. The result describes those groups, rather than the individual records we started with.

title: Which Assets Keep Returning with the Same Finding?
blurb: A report can ask which groups have enough evidence to meet a condition. WHERE determines which individual rows contribute; HAVING checks the groups after their summaries are calculated. Putting a condition at the wrong stage changes what we count.

title: Which Site Does Each Inspection Belong To?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Related facts often live in separate tables. An inner join places matching records together using a shared key. Each matching pair produces a result row, so repeated keys can change both the size and meaning of the report.

title: Which Assets Have No Matching Inspection?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Missing matches can be the information a report needs most. A left join retains every row from the starting table, including those without a qualifying match. Its missing-value placeholders need care when we filter or count the result.

title: Why Did Joining Readings Double the Inspection Total?
topic: Connecting Tables Without Changing the Question
blurb: Joining two collections of events can repeat each event across several matching pairs. A total over those pairs may count the same work more than once. Defining what each result row should describe tells us where to summarize before joining.

title: Which Inspections Took Longer Than the Usual Visit?
blurb: A query can use another query's result as part of its calculation or condition. That result might be one value or many rows. It can also depend on the current outer row, which changes the comparison being made.

title: Which Pumps Still Have No Completed Visit?
blurb: Sometimes we only need to know whether a related record is present. EXISTS answers that question without adding a result row for every match. Missing keys need particular care when we ask which records have no qualifying match.

title: Which Pumps Appear on Either List but Are Still Unfinished?
blurb: Separate queries can return overlapping collections of records. SQL can combine those results or find the rows that differ between them. We need compatible column meanings and an explicit choice about whether repeated results should remain.

title: Can We Read the Query in the Order We Explain the Job?
blurb: A complicated query becomes easier to follow when its intermediate results have names. Common table expressions let later stages refer to those results. Naming a stage helps explain its rows, but does not necessarily mean the database stores it separately.

title: How Far Does the Failed Supply Line Reach?
blurb: A hierarchy can have more levels than we know in advance. A recursive query starts with known rows and repeatedly follows their relationships. It also needs a stopping rule, especially when the records contain cycles or the search grows too large.

title: Keep Every Reading While Looking at Its Neighbors
blurb: Some calculations need neighboring records while retaining each individual row. Window functions define which rows belong together and how to order them for a comparison. This supports rankings or previous-value comparisons without reducing the whole group to one summary.

title: Which Readings Belong in This Rolling Total?
blurb: A running calculation depends on which neighboring rows contribute to each answer. A window frame defines that boundary. The last few records can cover a very different interval from the last few days, especially with tied timestamps or gaps.

title: Where Did the Quiet Day Go?
blurb: Reporting by date requires an agreed time zone and precise interval boundaries. Adjacent intervals should not count the same event twice. A calendar also supplies the dates absent from an event log, so quiet days remain visible in the report.

title: Why Did a Pump Search Return the Wrong Equipment?
blurb: Text comparisons depend on how we interpret spacing, letter case and special pattern characters. A search can return plausible but unintended matches. We need a consistent comparison policy without assuming that cleaning two names proves they identify the same thing.

title: Is That Temperature a Number or Just Text?
blurb: JSON lets a table store nested information, but extracting a field does not establish what it means. A numeric-looking string differs from a number. Validation and type checks keep those values separate from missing fields or explicit nulls.

title: What Could the Model Have Known at That Moment?
blurb: Historical training data should contain only information available at the decision being modeled. The time a measurement happened can differ from when it became usable. Both boundaries matter when joining records into model inputs and keeping future outcomes separate.

title: What Does One Equipment Record Promise?
blurb: A table needs an agreement about what its rows describe and what its fields mean. A schema records that structure. Choosing identifiers and units makes the stored values interpretable, while the database's actual type rules determine what it will accept.

title: Can a Job Refer to a Pump We Have Never Recorded?
blurb: A record can contain valid-looking values and still refer to something that does not exist. Database constraints reject writes that break declared rules. They help every writer preserve the same requirements for identifiers and relationships between records.

title: Why Must a Pump Move Be Edited on Every Job?
blurb: Repeating a shared fact across many rows creates several places to update it. Those copies can disagree. Normalization examines which identity determines each fact, so current information has a deliberate home while genuine historical records retain their meaning.

title: Change the Requested Jobs Without Rewriting the Rest
blurb: Changing data requires a precise definition of which records should change. SQL can add rows or modify existing ones, but a valid statement can still target the wrong set. Repeated imports also need a policy for existing identities and newer versions.

title: Move Spare Parts Without Losing Half the Transfer
blurb: One operation can require several related database changes. A transaction gives those changes a shared boundary, so a failure need not leave half the operation committed. Its rollback applies to work inside that boundary, rather than external effects such as messages already sent.

title: What If Someone Changes the Job While Botie Is Reading It?
blurb: A record can change between reading it and saving an edit. Checking an expected version helps detect that stale assumption. Database isolation provides further guarantees, whose scope matters when a decision depends on more than one row.

title: Find One Pump’s Readings Without Checking Every Pump
blurb: An index keeps an additional structure organized by selected values, giving a query a way to locate records without checking the whole table. Its ordering determines which lookups benefit, and every change to the data may require maintaining that structure.

title: Why Does a Short Query Repeat So Much Work?
blurb: A small result can require a large amount of database work. Query plans show the operations used to produce it, including repeated scans. We can use that evidence to investigate a rewrite while checking that the answer stays the same.

title: Let a Search Value Stay a Value
blurb: User-supplied text should remain a value rather than become part of a query's instructions. Parameter binding preserves that separation. Access rules still need to determine whose records the caller may read and which operations the application may perform.

title: Which Sensor Records Should Reach the Training Table?
blurb: A successful query can use records that violate the dataset's assumptions. Explicit checks expose invalid values or repeated identities before they affect model features. Keeping rejected evidence lets us investigate the problem instead of silently changing the training population.

title: Pick Up New Changes Without Losing Late Readings
blurb: Importing only new changes can save work, but event timestamps alone can miss late arrivals and corrections. A repeatable pipeline needs a source change position and record versions. Its checkpoint must advance with the changes that actually reached the destination.

title: Which Records Does the Technician Need Together?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: The way records are stored affects which requests are straightforward and which require extra work. A key lookup and a report across many records make different demands. Those access patterns give us a reason to compare database designs.

title: Which P1 Did the Lookup Mean?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A key gives a stored value the name used to retrieve it. That name needs enough information to distinguish records from different sources. We also need to distinguish an absent key from a stored value of zero.

title: How Long Should Botie Trust the Saved Reading?
topic: Choosing the Shape of the Records
blurb: A cache keeps a copy of an earlier answer so we can reuse it. That copy can become outdated while it is still available. An expiry policy limits reuse, but the service must also handle requests when the cached answer is missing.

title: Can One Record Describe the Pump and Its Sensor?
blurb: A document groups named fields and can contain nested records or arrays. That structure can keep related details together, but readers still need rules for the values. An omitted field and an explicit null may communicate different information.

title: Should Every Pump Keep a Copy of the Supplier’s Phone Number?
blurb: Keeping related details inside one document can save a lookup. Copying a shared fact into many documents also creates copies to maintain. Distinguishing current information from an intentional historical snapshot helps us decide what to embed and what to reference.

title: Did the High Value Belong to the Temperature Sensor?
blurb: Conditions on an array need to describe the same member when their evidence belongs together. Otherwise, separate members can satisfy separate conditions and produce a misleading match. A document query must preserve that relationship as it selects records.

title: Can Botie Save a Change Without Erasing Somebody Else’s?
blurb: Saving a whole document can erase changes made by another editor. A targeted update changes only the intended fields, while an expected version checks whether the reviewed state is still current. The database must enforce that condition with the write.

title: Can We Find North’s Hot Pumps Without Reading Every Document?
blurb: An index helps a document query locate a smaller set of possible matches. Conditions not answered by the index still need checking. The useful arrangement depends on the requests being made, as well as the cost of maintaining the index.

title: How Much Urgent Work Was Hidden Inside the Pump Documents?
blurb: A document report can pass records through several transformations. Expanding an array changes what one row represents, which affects later totals. Following that meaning through each stage helps us avoid counting the same parent record several times.

title: Why Is One Storage Key Doing All the Work?
topic: Partitioning for the Questions We Ask
blurb: A partition key groups records so the system can direct related work to the right place. A convenient grouping can also concentrate too many requests. Choosing the key requires understanding the traffic as well as the data being stored.

title: Keep One Asset’s History Together Without Growing Forever
topic: Partitioning for the Questions We Ask
blurb: A request for one entity's history needs an efficient way to locate the relevant time range. Wide-column designs combine a partition key with an ordering inside that partition. Time buckets can keep each group bounded as the history grows.

title: Why Did the Repair Disappear When Botie Read It Back?
blurb: Replicas hold copies of the same data, but an update may reach them at different times. A consistency contract defines what a reader can expect to observe. That promise determines which copy may answer and when waiting or failure is necessary.

title: Two Technicians Cannot Both Reserve the Last Kit
blurb: Reading a value does not reserve it for a later change. A conditional write checks whether the required state still holds when the update is applied. This lets competing requests reject a stale decision instead of overwriting each other's work.

title: How Can Two Offline Teams Keep Both Inspection Counts?
blurb: Disconnected writers can each change their own copy of a value. Keeping a separate contribution for each writer gives a grow-only counter enough information to merge those changes repeatedly. A safe merge depends on what the value represents.

title: Why Does the Dashboard Still Count a Job That Was Closed?
blurb: A projection stores a view derived from source records for a particular request. A change stream can keep that view current, provided the consumer handles repeated or out-of-order changes. Record versions help prevent old updates from undoing newer information.

title: The New Sensor Sends a Different Document
blurb: A document collection can accept a new structure while older readers still expect the previous one. Explicit representation versions let software interpret both deliberately. A compatible reader needs to understand the fields before converting their values into a common form.

title: The Bad Update Reached Every Replica. What Can We Restore?
blurb: Replication can copy an accidental change to every replica. Recovery needs retained history from before the mistake. A snapshot and a complete interval of changes can reconstruct a chosen state, which still needs checking before readers use it.

title: A Fast Feature Lookup Still Has to Mean the Right Thing
blurb: A fast feature lookup is useful only if its values mean what the model expects. A serving record needs a matching feature definition and sufficiently recent observations in the declared order. Historical training records need their own record of what was available then.

title: Which Equipment Depends on This Supply?
blurb: A graph database stores relationships between records explicitly. The direction and meaning of each connection determine what we can infer by following it. This is useful when the question depends on how entities are connected, rather than their properties alone.

title: Are These Two Pumps Actually the Same Pump?
blurb: A shared name does not establish that two records describe the same entity. Graph connections need identifiers with a clear scope that remain useful when a label changes. Otherwise, merging records can attach relationships to the wrong thing.

title: Who Inspected This Pump?
blurb: A graph query can describe a connected pattern and find the records that fit it. Variables retain the identity of each matched node, so following another relationship continues from the same record instead of combining unrelated matches.

title: How Many Inspections Were Actually Completed?
blurb: A graph query can find several routes to the same record. Counting those matches answers a different question from counting distinct entities. The filters and grouping need to reflect what each matched row actually describes.

title: Keep the Pumps That Have No Completed Inspection
blurb: A required graph pattern returns only successful matches. An optional pattern can retain the starting entity when a relationship is absent, making missing information visible. We need to distinguish that preserved placeholder from a real matched record when counting results.

title: Follow a Dependency Without Following It Forever
blurb: Following relationships can lead back to a node already visited. A traversal needs to distinguish finding reachable entities from listing every route to them. Remembering visited nodes prevents repeated exploration, while a depth limit states how far the search actually went.

title: The Route with Fewer Stops Takes Longer
blurb: The route with the fewest connections may take longer to travel. A weighted search compares accumulated costs instead of counting edges. Dijkstra's algorithm finds minimum-cost routes when those costs are nonnegative, with explicit treatment of unreachable destinations.

title: Which Rules Must Every Asset Write Preserve?
blurb: Graph records need enforceable rules for identity, including whether a key must be present and unique. Constraints protect those rules when data changes. Indexes support lookups, while existing duplicates need investigation before an identity constraint can be installed.

title: The Graph Changed While the Approval Was Waiting
blurb: An approved graph change can become stale while another writer updates the same entity. The final transaction needs to check current state and permissions before committing. Preparing or reviewing a snapshot alone cannot protect the later write from concurrent changes.

title: A Replayed Import Must Not Create Another Relationship
blurb: Retrying an import should recognize relationships already applied. Stable identities let us distinguish an exact replay from a conflicting record. Missing endpoints and invalid rows need an explicit rejection path so the graph does not silently lose or duplicate connections.

title: Why Did One More Hop Make the Query So Expensive?
blurb: A graph query can return a few records after exploring many connections. Its starting point and intermediate matches determine much of that work. Query plans help us investigate the search, while representative measurements are needed to assess actual performance.

title: Can Two Teams Describe the Same Resource?
blurb: Combining datasets requires a clear way to name resources and state their relationships. RDF represents those statements using resource identifiers and literal values. SPARQL matches patterns of statements, with rules that differ from a property-graph query.

title: Where Did This Maintenance Claim Come From?
blurb: A claim becomes easier to assess when we retain its source and the period it applies to. Recording claims separately lets contradictory evidence remain visible. We can then choose relevant information without treating the last imported statement as established truth.

title: Which Connected Records Can the Assistant Use?
blurb: Connected records can give an assistant context that an isolated document lacks. Retrieval still needs limits on which paths it follows and what evidence the user may access. Historical evaluations also need to exclude information unavailable at the original decision.

title: What Does One Row Represent?
blurb: A row needs a clear meaning before its values can be counted or compared. Record identities help us distinguish duplicate imports from genuine repeated observations and preserve the evidence behind corrections.

title: When a Measurement Is Missing
blurb: A missing measurement tells us that information is unavailable. Replacing it with a value keeps a calculation running, but the replacement introduces an assumption that can affect the conclusions we draw from the data.

title: Categories Without an Invented Ranking
blurb: Category names identify different kinds of things without necessarily putting them in an order. Separate membership columns let us calculate with those categories while preserving their meaning and avoiding invented numerical distances.

title: When the End Is Beside the Beginning
blurb: Hours and seasons repeat, so values at opposite ends of their numbering can be close together. Representing a cycle with coordinates on a circle preserves that relationship when we calculate distances or fit a model.

title: What Could We Know at Prediction Time?
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: Evaluation becomes misleading when a prediction uses information that would only become available later. Reconstructing what was known at the decision time helps us test a procedure that can actually be used.

title: When the Important Class Is Rare
topic: Keep Future Answers Out of Training
blurb: When one outcome is much more common than another, overall accuracy can conceal failures on the rare outcome. Looking at errors within each class makes those failures visible and helps us choose an appropriate evaluation.

title: What Must a Model Improve On?
blurb: A simple prediction rule gives us a reference for judging a more complicated one. Comparing both on the same new observations shows whether the additional work produces a useful improvement.

title: Would More Examples Help?
blurb: Training and validation errors can change differently as more examples become available. Following both helps us decide whether collecting more data is a useful next experiment or whether the model itself needs attention.

title: When Should a Probability Become an Action?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A predicted probability becomes an action only after we decide what level justifies acting. The consequences of missed events and unnecessary actions affect where that threshold should be set.

title: Does Eighty Percent Mean Eighty Percent?
topic: From a Score to a Decision
blurb: A probability has a practical meaning when outcomes occur at roughly the rates it predicts. Calibration compares predicted chances with observed frequencies, helping us judge whether those probabilities support reliable decisions.

title: Have We Really Held Out a New Example?
blurb: Records from the same person or device can share information. Keeping those groups together when separating training and evaluation gives us a better test of performance on groups the model has not encountered.

title: What Changed After the Model Was Fitted?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: The data arriving after a system is released can differ from the data used to develop it. Comparing populations helps us find changes worth investigating; their effect on prediction quality still needs to be measured.

title: How Much Does Our Estimate Depend on This Sample?
topic: Know the Limits of the Result
blurb: An estimate depends on which observations were collected. Repeatedly sampling from the observed data and recalculating the estimate helps us examine that variation, provided the resampling respects how the observations are related.

title: What Are the Errors Trying to Tell Us?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: Prediction errors have direction as well as size, so positive and negative errors can cancel in an average. Examining each error alongside its inputs helps reveal conditions under which a model repeatedly misses the outcome.

title: Which Alerts Deserve an Inspection?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: Precision measures how many positive predictions are correct, while recall measures how many actual positives are found. Changing a decision threshold affects both and changes the amount of work generated by an alert system.

title: Better for Which Cases?
topic: Find the Mistakes Behind the Score
blurb: An overall score can improve while performance worsens for a particular group. Comparing errors within meaningful subsets and keeping their sizes visible helps us judge who benefits from a revision and where uncertainty remains.

title: Did the Revision Help on the Same Cases?
blurb: A model revision needs to be compared with its predecessor on the same cases. Paired errors preserve which observations improved or worsened, and resampling those pairs helps examine uncertainty in the difference.

title: Who Checks the Model-Choosing Process?
blurb: Searching many settings can make the best validation score look better than the selection procedure really is. An outer evaluation kept separate from that search tests the process of choosing and fitting a model.

title: Is the Model Wrong, or Is the Record Wrong?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: An apparent prediction error may begin with an incorrect label or a mismatched record. Reviewing disagreements from predictions made without fitting those records helps prioritize investigation while preserving the original evidence and evaluation boundaries.

title: When Should the Model Ask for Help?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: Referring uncertain predictions for human review changes which cases the model handles. Measuring both accepted-case errors and the volume of referrals shows whether the policy improves the whole system rather than simply moving its workload.

title: Should This Change the Prediction?
topic: Repair the Evidence and the Behaviour
blurb: A change of units or batch composition can alter an input's representation without changing its meaning. Testing the complete prediction procedure against those changes helps check that preparation and model behavior remain consistent.

title: Repair the Night-Shift Model Without Breaking the Day Shift
topic: Build and Check a Model Revision
blurb: A model repair needs a specific explanation for the errors it is meant to reduce. Comparing the revision on shared cases and a fresh dataset checks whether the intended improvement survives group-performance and runtime requirements.

title: What Does an Alarm Tell Us?
blurb: New information changes which possibilities we should consider. Conditional probability accounts for that information, including how common an event was before the new evidence arrived.

title: Which Rule Could Have Produced These Observations?
blurb: Likelihood compares proposed rules by how plausible they make the observations we already have. Varying a rule's parameters while keeping the data fixed gives us a way to choose settings that fit those observations.

title: Naive Bayes
blurb: Naive Bayes combines evidence from several measurements to estimate a category. Its simplifying assumption treats those measurements as independent within each category, making the calculation manageable while limiting which relationships it can describe.

title: Support Vector Machines and Margins
blurb: Several boundaries may separate the same labeled observations. A support vector machine prefers a wider gap between the classes while allowing a controlled cost for observations that fall inside that gap or on the wrong side.

title: Hierarchical Clustering
blurb: Small groups can form parts of larger groups. Hierarchical clustering records that structure by joining nearby groups in stages, leaving us a hierarchy to examine before choosing one level of grouping.

title: Density-Based Clustering
blurb: Dense neighborhoods allow a cluster to grow through connected points. Density-based clustering can follow irregular groups while leaving isolated observations unassigned, with the result depending on what counts as nearby and sufficiently dense.

title: Images as Arrays
blurb: A digital image stores measurements at ordered pixel positions. Rows and columns preserve location, while color channels describe each pixel's values. The number type affects what calculations can safely do to those measurements.

title: Image Thresholding
blurb: A threshold selects pixels whose values meet a cutoff and records those decisions in a mask. This can separate a region from its background when their intensities differ enough, but lighting changes can make one cutoff unreliable.

title: Cleaning Masks With Morphology
blurb: Morphological operations use a small shape to examine neighboring pixels in a mask. They can remove isolated marks or connect regions, while also changing boundaries that may matter to later measurements.

title: Connected Components
blurb: Selected pixels form a region only when they are connected under a chosen neighbor rule. Labeling each connected region lets us count and measure it separately, without assuming that every region represents one physical object.

title: Image Augmentation
blurb: A training image can be transformed into additional examples when the transformation preserves the task's meaning. Spatial labels must move with the image, and related versions must stay together when separating training from evaluation.

title: Transfer Learning
blurb: A previously trained network may already represent useful visual patterns. Reusing those representations lets us test a smaller new predictor before deciding whether changing the earlier network layers is justified by the available data.

title: Bounding Boxes and Overlap
blurb: Bounding boxes describe where an object appears in an image. Their coordinates need a consistent convention, and the overlap between a predicted box and a labeled box gives us one way to measure localization.

title: Non-Maximum Suppression
blurb: An object detector can produce several overlapping guesses for one object. Non-maximum suppression keeps higher-scoring boxes and removes nearby alternatives according to an overlap threshold, which can also affect detections of neighboring objects.

title: What Would We Predict Before Fitting Anything?
blurb: Recent observations and historical averages provide simple forecasts that can be made before the next value is known. Their errors give more complicated forecasting methods a reference to improve on.

title: Building Inputs From Earlier Days
blurb: Earlier observations can become inputs for predicting a later value. Keeping those inputs aligned with their target and actual availability prevents a forecast from accidentally using the answer it is meant to predict.

title: Separating Repetition From Change
blurb: A series can change because of a lasting trend or a repeating cycle. Comparing each value with a relevant earlier value helps separate those patterns and changes what remains for a forecasting method to explain.

title: Updating a Forecast Without Starting Over
blurb: A running estimate can give recent observations more influence while retaining information from earlier ones. Exponential smoothing controls how quickly that estimate responds, making its response to change a deliberate choice.

title: Learning From a Series' Own Past
blurb: An autoregressive model predicts a series from its own earlier values. Fitted coefficients give those past values different influence, and using predictions as later inputs can carry errors further into the forecast.

title: Testing a Forecast as Time Moves Forward
blurb: A forecast must be judged using only the information available when it would have been made. Repeating that check at several dates shows how methods perform as the observed history grows and conditions change.

title: Trying an Action Before Knowing Its Value
blurb: Trying an action reveals its outcome while leaving the alternatives uncertain. A bandit strategy balances using the action that currently looks best with gathering evidence about choices that have been tried less often.

title: Describing What an Action Changes
blurb: An action changes the situation in which the next decision will be made. States describe the relevant conditions, and transition probabilities describe the possible consequences of acting under those conditions.

title: Valuing Rewards That Arrive Later
blurb: The value of an action can depend on rewards that arrive much later. A return combines rewards over time, with discounting controlling how strongly later rewards influence the comparison between choices.

title: Planning One Step, Then the Remaining Journey
blurb: A decision's value combines its immediate reward with the value of the situations it may lead to. When transition probabilities are known, repeated updates to those estimates give us a way to compare longer sequences of decisions.

title: Learning Action Values From Experience
blurb: Action values can be updated from observed outcomes even when transition probabilities are unknown. Q-learning combines a received reward with an estimate of the best continuation, then uses the difference to revise the chosen action's value.

title: Planning for More Than One Possible Outcome
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A probability distribution keeps possible outcomes beside their chances. Weighting each outcome by its probability gives an expectation, which helps compare uncertain decisions without assuming that the average must occur in any individual case.

title: Updating an Unknown Failure Rate
topic: Describing What We Do Not Know
blurb: A small sample can support several plausible values for an unknown rate. A posterior distribution combines prior assumptions with the observed results, preserving uncertainty about that rate as more evidence arrives.

title: Combining Measurements With Different Reliability
blurb: When measurement errors are independent and have no systematic offset, their known variances tell us how strongly to weight each reading. Under the Gaussian model, the combined estimate also describes the uncertainty that remains.

title: Tracking a State We Cannot Observe Directly
blurb: A system's condition may be hidden while its measurements are noisy. Filtering predicts how that condition could change, then updates the possible states using the evidence in each new observation.

title: Predicting Between Measurements With Uncertainty
blurb: Gaussian processes connect observed and unobserved values through assumptions about how those values vary together. Conditioning on measurements gives predictions with remaining uncertainty, both of which depend on those assumptions and the measurement noise.

title: Learning From a Few Records at a Time
blurb: Using a subset of training records reduces the work needed for each parameter update. The resulting gradient estimates vary between batches, so batch size affects both the computational cost and the variability of training.

title: Remembering the Direction of Earlier Updates
blurb: Successive updates can point in different directions because of the data or the shape of the objective. Momentum carries part of the earlier update direction forward, giving the next adjustment some memory of previous steps.

title: Giving Different Weights Different Step Scales
blurb: Parameters can receive gradients with very different sizes. Adam keeps running averages of each gradient and its square, using that history to scale parameter updates while accounting for the averages' initial values.

title: Checking a Model Before a Long Training Run
blurb: A network's starting values affect how signals move through it. Separately checking its derivatives against small numerical changes helps distinguish a calculation error from a training problem before a long run begins.

title: Deciding When a Training Run Has Done Enough
blurb: Lower training error does not always produce better predictions on new records. Comparing training and validation curves supports a stopping rule and helps us decide when to change the learning rate or restore an earlier model.

title: Recommending Something Before Knowing the Reader
blurb: Interaction counts provide a simple recommendation rule when little is known about a new user. Their meaning depends on which items people had a chance to see, so popularity reflects exposure as well as preference.

title: Matching a Reader’s Interests to Guide Descriptions
blurb: An item's description can help identify who might find it useful before anyone has rated it. Representing item properties and a user's interests in the same coordinates makes that comparison possible, subject to what the descriptions capture.

title: Learning From Readers With Similar Preferences
blurb: People who agree on some items may provide useful evidence about others. Collaborative filtering uses those shared ratings to compare preferences, while keeping an absent rating distinct from a negative opinion.

title: Compressing a Sparse Table of Preferences
blurb: A large rating table often contains many unobserved entries. Small vectors for users and items can capture shared patterns in the observed ratings, allowing predictions to reuse information across the table.

title: Checking the List a Reader Actually Sees
blurb: The usefulness of a recommendation depends on the short list a person actually sees. Relevant items and their positions need to be evaluated against a defined candidate set, including situations with little earlier interaction history.

title: Finding Unusual Readings Without Letting Them Set the Reference
blurb: Extreme observations can move the average and spread used to judge them. References based on medians and absolute deviations reduce that influence, helping us identify unusual readings without treating every unusual value as a fault.

title: Judging a Reading Against Its Neighbors
blurb: An observation can be unusual relative to its neighbors even when it fits a broader range. Local outlier factor compares surrounding densities, allowing different parts of a dataset to have different ordinary levels of variation.

title: Finding Readings That Are Easy to Separate
blurb: An observation far from the others is often separated by fewer random splits. Isolation forests combine those path lengths across trees to score unusual observations, leaving the meaning of an alert to a separate investigation.

title: Detecting Patterns a Model Cannot Reconstruct
blurb: A model trained to reproduce reference patterns can make larger reconstruction errors on unfamiliar ones. Those errors provide an anomaly score whose usefulness depends on the reference data and a separately checked alert threshold.

title: Recording Which Things Are Connected
blurb: A graph records which objects are connected as well as what is known about each object. Consistent identities and edge directions let calculations use those relationships without confusing the objects or the meaning of their connections.

title: Following Probability Through a Network
blurb: A random walk assigns probabilities to the next connection taken from each location. Following those probabilities reveals how network structure affects where a walk can reach and where it may remain or keep cycling.

title: Letting a Node Read Its Neighbors’ Measurements
blurb: Connected objects can provide context about one another. Aggregating their measurements combines that context while preserving each object's identity; choosing a sum or a mean changes how the number of connections affects the result.

title: Learning From a Node and Its Neighbors Together
blurb: A graph convolution combines an object's measurements with information from its neighbors. Scaling for the number of connections controls their influence, while learned weights determine how the combined features contribute to the next representation.

title: Scoring Connections We Have Not Observed
blurb: Representations of connected objects can be used to score possible missing links. An unrecorded connection may simply be unobserved, so candidate selection and the separation of training from evaluation affect what those scores can establish.

title: Separating a Useful Prediction From a Causal Claim
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: A treatment and an outcome can share causes that make them appear related. Understanding those common causes helps distinguish a useful prediction from evidence that changing the treatment would change the outcome.

title: Making a Fair Comparison by Assignment
topic: Asking What a Change Would Do
blurb: Random assignment separates a treatment choice from the reasons someone might otherwise select it. Comparing outcomes by assignment helps estimate an average causal effect, with uncertainty that depends on the experiment's design and size.

title: Comparing Treatments in the Same Population
blurb: Different treatment groups may begin with different conditions. Standardization compares their outcomes using the same target population, provided the measured conditions account for the relevant common causes and both treatments have adequate representation.

title: Reweighting Records Without Inventing Missing Evidence
blurb: Inverse-probability weighting gives more influence to outcomes from cases less likely to receive their observed treatment. The comparison depends on credible treatment probabilities and enough overlap to support both treatment choices in the population of interest.

title: Saving the Whole Prediction Procedure
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: Reproducing a prediction requires the fitted preparation and input conventions as well as model parameters. Saving the complete procedure and checking it after loading helps preserve the meaning of a prediction across processes.

title: Checking What Arrives at the Model
topic: From Training to a Repeatable Prediction
blurb: A numerically valid input can still have the wrong meaning. Named fields and explicit units help a prediction service check requests before calculation, making errors in feature order or missing values visible to the caller.

title: Keeping a Prediction Consistent Across Requests
blurb: Prediction code should apply the same fitted preparation to a record whether it arrives alone or in a batch. Keeping shared state from changing during requests prevents accidental differences between the two.

title: Knowing Which Model Produced an Answer
blurb: A prediction needs to be traceable to the model and preparation that produced it. Recording the associated data and code versions makes a past result easier to investigate and provides a reproducible target for rollback.

title: Checking the Model After It Meets New Data
blurb: A released system can encounter new data or changed operating conditions. Separating service measurements from prediction-quality checks helps identify the problem, while a compatible saved procedure provides a route back when a revision fails.

title: Investigate a Sensor Before Calling It Faulty
blurb: An alert procedure turns unusual sensor readings into requests for investigation. Its reference and threshold need to be chosen before evaluating later labeled cases, so the reported performance reflects decisions that could actually have been made.

title: Forecast Tomorrow’s Water Demand Without Seeing Tomorrow
blurb: A useful demand forecast must be available before the demand itself is observed. Comparing a fitted model with simple persistence at matching forecast dates helps reveal whether the additional complexity improves planning.

title: Count Seeds While Keeping the Image Assumptions Visible
blurb: Counting seeds from an image depends on separating their pixels into distinct regions. Thresholding and connected components provide a small, inspectable procedure whose failures reveal when dust or touching seeds violate its assumptions.

title: What Would This Prediction Actually Change?
blurb: A prediction is useful when it informs an action someone can take. Starting with that decision helps define the required information and measurable limits the proposed system needs to meet.

title: Do We Need a Learned Model Yet?
blurb: An existing rule gives us a baseline for deciding whether machine learning adds useful value. Comparing its consequences and upkeep with a learned model makes the additional benefit and cost visible.

title: What Can the System Know at Decision Time?
blurb: The time an event occurred differs from the time its record became available. A system's input requirements need to account for both, so a past decision is not evaluated using information it could not have received.

title: Where Does the Prediction Pipeline Run Out of Room?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: A processing pipeline can finish work only as quickly as its limiting stage allows. Comparing the capacity of preparation and prediction with the surrounding operations helps identify which change would improve the whole service.

title: What Happens When Requests Arrive Together?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: A queue holds work that has arrived but has not finished processing. Short bursts can create a long wait even when average demand is manageable, so capacity estimates need to follow unfinished work over time.

title: Will the Model Fit on the Device?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: A running model needs memory for intermediate calculations and its execution environment as well as saved parameters. Those additional demands affect which model and batch sizes will fit on a device.

title: Should the Prediction Happen Here or on a Server?
section: Model the System Before Building It
blurb: Local and remote prediction divide the work differently between a device and a server. Communication time and connection failures affect that choice alongside computing speed, with separate consequences for energy use and data exposure.

title: Which Designs Are Actually Acceptable?
blurb: A design must meet its required limits before its advantages can make it useful. Filtering by those requirements separates unacceptable options from choices that involve a genuine tradeoff between objectives.

title: Which Assumption Could Change Our Decision?
blurb: A design decision can depend heavily on an uncertain estimate. Varying plausible inputs shows which assumptions could change the preferred design and which new measurement would be most useful.

title: What Should the Prototype Teach Us?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: A prototype provides evidence about a design choice before the complete system is built. Testing related factors together can reveal interactions, where the effect of one choice depends on the setting of another.

title: What Should Happen When the Model Cannot Help?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: An unavailable model or unusable input still leaves the application with a decision to handle. A fallback defines what happens in those conditions, including where unresolved cases go and how the system returns to normal operation.

title: Can We Defend the Inspection Service Design?
section: Test the Design and Plan for Failure
blurb: A complete service needs evidence for its operating requirements as well as its prediction results. Checking missed faults alongside the workload they generate shows whether an inspection design fits the team's actual capacity.

title: What Makes This an Agent?
topic: From an Answer to an Action
blurb: An agent uses a model's output to choose a next step, such as requesting information from a tool. The surrounding program performs that operation and returns its result, giving the model new information for the next decision.

title: How Do We Give an Agent a Job It Can Follow?
topic: Giving the Model a Clear Job
blurb: A prompt gives a language model its task and the information available to answer it. Clear instructions and examples make the requested behavior easier to test, including what the answer should say when evidence is missing.

title: Can Another Program Use Botie’s Answer?
topic: Giving the Model a Clear Job
blurb: Structured outputs put a model's response into fields another program can read. Checking their types and required values catches malformed records, while the accuracy of the information in those fields needs a separate check.

title: When May Botie Turn a Suggestion into an Action?
blurb: A tool gives an agent access to an operation performed by another program. Its interface needs to define acceptable inputs and permissions, including how repeated requests are handled when the operation changes stored data.

title: Which Records Should Botie Bring into the Conversation?
blurb: A model can process only a limited amount of information in one request. Selecting relevant, permitted records and retaining their sources helps use that space without losing the evidence needed to support the answer.

title: What Should Botie Do After a Tool Replies?
blurb: An agent loop lets a model choose another step after receiving a tool's result. The program keeps track of those steps and decides when to stop, retry a recoverable failure, or ask a person for help.

title: Does Botie Need to Choose the Next Step?
topic: Choosing How Much Autonomy to Give
blurb: A fixed workflow chooses its steps in code, while an agent lets a model choose some steps from the results it observes. That additional freedom is useful when the task requires it, and adds behavior the application needs to test.

title: Give Botie a Typed Job with Pydantic AI
blurb: Pydantic AI organizes model calls around declared inputs and outputs, with tools for requesting information. Those declarations help the surrounding program check a response, while its factual support still depends on the evidence returned.

title: Put Limits Around a LangChain Agent
blurb: LangChain coordinates the messages and tool calls in an agent run. Explicit limits on those calls help control repeated attempts, while the recorded messages show what information the agent used at each step.

title: Resume Botie’s Work with LangGraph
blurb: LangGraph represents a workflow as connected operations with saved state. That state lets work continue after a pause, but resuming it still requires clear rules for merging changes and avoiding repeated external actions.

title: Ask Before Botie Creates the Inspection Job
blurb: Human approval connects a proposed action to a person's decision about it. The program performing the action needs to confirm that its details still match the proposal and that the approval remains valid.

title: Connect Botie to Tools with MCP
blurb: The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, gives applications a shared way to discover and call tools supplied by other programs. A common interface simplifies the connection while leaving permissions and the interpretation of returned information to the application.

title: What If the Manual Starts Giving Botie Orders?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: Prompt injection occurs when supplied content tries to redirect a model's instructions. Documents and tool results can carry those attempts, so the application still needs to enforce permissions when a model follows an instruction it should have ignored.

title: Whose Pump Is Botie Allowed to Inspect?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: Authorization determines what an authenticated caller may do with a particular record. Allowing a tool by name is insufficient when its arguments can point to another person's information or a different customer's resources.

title: How Much of the Maintenance Record Does Botie Need?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: Permission to read information does not automatically include permission to send it to another service. Restricting a request to the fields its task needs reduces unnecessary disclosure, including through logs and saved conversations.

title: Can We Safely Use the Answer Botie Returned?
topic: Guardrails at the Point of Action
blurb: A model's response becomes input to the program that uses it. Its contents need checks appropriate to that use, including whether identifiers match the request and whether displayed text could be interpreted as executable markup.

title: Did Botie Create the Inspection, or Did the Reply Get Lost?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: A timed-out request may have completed even though its reply never arrived. A stable action identity and a way to recover the receiver's result help prevent a retry from performing the same operation twice.

title: Can Two of Botie’s Calls Spend the Same Remaining Budget?
topic: Keeping an Agent Run Under Control
blurb: Concurrent tool calls can each appear to fit a budget while exceeding it together. Reserving resources before dispatch makes unfinished work part of the limit, including the time and cost already committed to other calls.

title: Which Examples Should We Put in the Prompt?
blurb: Examples in a prompt show the relationship between a request and an acceptable response. Their selection affects what distinctions the model is shown, so their usefulness needs to be checked on other requests.

title: Why Did Botie Take So Long?
blurb: A trace records the operations that contributed to one request, with their timing and relationships. It helps explain where an agent spent time or repeated work without relying on the final answer to describe its execution.

title: Can We Find the Run Behind This Score?
blurb: Langfuse records agent executions and connects them to prompt versions and evaluation scores. Keeping those identities together lets us inspect the answers behind a reported improvement and see which runs were actually evaluated.

title: What Would Count as Doing the Job?
blurb: An evaluation dataset pairs tasks with the conditions and results expected from them. For an agent, those expectations can include permitted actions and failure behavior as well as the final answer.

title: What Can We Test Without Calling a Model?
topic: Testing the Program Around the Model
blurb: A test model supplies controlled responses without contacting a real model provider. This lets us check how an agent program handles arguments and tool results, while answer quality still requires evaluation with the intended model.

title: Who Checks the Model That Checks Botie?
blurb: A model judge evaluates an answer against a written set of criteria. Its decisions can vary with the wording or presentation, so agreement with human review needs to be checked before relying on its scores.

title: Where Did the Answer First Go Wrong?
blurb: Error analysis traces a failed answer back through the information and operations that produced it. Distinguishing missing evidence from a mistaken interpretation helps identify a repair worth testing instead of changing the prompt at random.

title: Did the New Examples Cause the Improvement?
blurb: Changing several parts of an agent at once can hide which change affected its performance. Comparing versions with individual changes on the same tasks helps separate their effects and reveal cases that became worse.

title: Is This Version Ready for the Next Shift?
blurb: A higher average score can conceal a new failure on an important task. Comparing agent versions on the same cases, with explicit requirements and operating limits, makes those tradeoffs visible before release.

title: Can We Make Botie Cross the Boundary?
blurb: Adversarial evaluations deliberately try to violate a stated rule. The useful evidence is what the agent actually did under those conditions, including whether its controls also blocked requests that should have been allowed.

title: What Happens When the New Shift Finds a Failure?
blurb: Stopping an agent prevents new work only if the stop reaches the programs performing its actions. Requests already in progress may still complete, so recovery also requires finding out what happened before resuming operation.

title: Repair Botie’s Maintenance Assistant
topic: A Repair From Failure to Fresh Evidence
blurb: An outdated source can produce a convincing answer with the wrong information. Repairing the retrieval rule and evaluating fresh requests connects the original failure to evidence that the revised application handles it better.

title: What Should Botie Be Unable to Do?
blurb: Guardrails limit the effects an agent can have on an application. Instructions describe the intended behavior, while checks where actions occur determine what the agent can actually do.

title: Can Botie Fix the Bug Without Rewriting the Rules?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: A coding agent can change the tests as well as the program being tested. Reviewing its complete patch and checking it independently helps keep the requested repair from weakening the requirements it was meant to satisfy.

title: Where Should Botie Run Code He Has Just Written?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: A sandbox restricts the files and services a running program can reach. Those limits matter when executing agent-written code, including code that attempts to read credentials or consume more resources than expected.

title: Are We Releasing the Code We Actually Checked?
topic: Working Safely with a Coding Agent
blurb: A release includes dependencies and build outputs as well as the code we edited. Review and test results need to identify those exact inputs and outputs, or they may describe a different program from the one being released.

title: What Did We Actually Trust When We Connected the MCP Server?
blurb: An MCP connection lets an application discover and use capabilities supplied by another program. The server's identity and the permissions granted to it matter even when its tools have familiar names.

title: A Valid Token for Which Service?
blurb: An access token identifies a grant of authority for a particular service. A valid token for one API does not give an MCP server permission to use it elsewhere or read every record it can reach.

title: What Exactly Did the Person Approve?
blurb: Approval applies to the action a person actually reviewed. If its target or details change before execution, the application needs to check that approval again and recognize a retry of the same action.

title: What Should Botie Pass to Another Agent?
blurb: Saved memory and delegated tasks can carry information into later agent runs. Their ownership and permissions need to remain clear so an old note or a handoff cannot grant new access.

title: Can the Repaired Agent Survive a Different Shift?
blurb: An agent's final answer may hide an unauthorized action taken earlier in the run. Testing the recorded effects against the intended permissions helps reveal those failures, along with legitimate work the controls prevented.

title: Names, Units, and Readable Code
blurb: A calculation can run correctly while leaving its meaning difficult to follow. Names, explicit units and useful documentation help another reader understand the assumptions they need to preserve.

title: Functions with Clear Responsibilities
blurb: A function is easier to reuse when its inputs and result describe one coherent job. Keeping calculations separate from display and external effects makes changes easier to reason about and test.

title: DRY and Shared Rules
blurb: Copies of the same rule can drift apart as requirements change. DRY keeps that knowledge in one place, while leaving unrelated operations separate when their reasons for changing differ.

title: Type Hints and Function Contracts
blurb: Type hints describe the values an interface expects and returns. Static tools can use that information to find incompatible uses, while runtime checks still decide whether external data is acceptable.

title: Missing Values, Defaults, and None
blurb: An absent setting, an explicit None and a measured zero can mean different things. Defaults and optional types need to preserve those distinctions so the program applies the intended policy.

title: Dataclasses and Record Ownership
blurb: A dataclass gives a recurring record a named Python type and generates common methods. Validation and ownership of mutable fields remain explicit design decisions.

title: Composition and Interchangeable Components
blurb: A program can combine small components through clear interfaces. Passing a dependency explicitly lets callers replace where data comes from or where results go without rewriting the calculation.

title: Fail Fast, Fail Early
blurb: A failure is easier to understand before invalid data produces a misleading result or changes saved records. Validate the contract at the boundary, then decide which failures the caller can recover from.

title: Pydantic Models and Optional Fields
blurb: A record can require a field, allow None as its value, or provide a default when the field is omitted. Pydantic turns those declared rules into runtime validation, so the difference stays explicit at a program boundary.

title: Pydantic Constraints and Validators
blurb: A correctly typed request can still ask for an impossible range or an unsuitable count. Express field limits, relationships and normalization explicitly, then route validation errors without hiding defects in the program.

title: Python Exceptions
blurb: An exception carries a failed operation back to a caller that may be able to handle it. Keep recovery specific, preserve the useful cause, and avoid disguising a defect as a successful result.

title: Mutation and Copies
blurb: Two names can refer to the same mutable object. Make ownership and copying explicit so an edit does not change another caller’s data or leak into a later function call.

title: Context Managers and Resource Cleanup
blurb: A file or connection needs a defined lifetime even when processing fails. Use with and context managers to keep acquisition and cleanup together without hiding the original error.

title: Testing Python Functions
blurb: A program can run without producing the right result. Tests preserve expectations about its behavior, including boundaries and earlier mistakes, so a change can be checked against those expectations.

title: Dependency Injection and Test Doubles
blurb: A report test is easier to repeat when its reading source is explicit. Controlled source and sink objects let us inspect data and calls locally, while separate integration checks exercise actual devices or services.

title: Modules and Project Structure
blurb: Modules give related code a clear home. Explicit imports and a separate entry point let us reuse a calculation without also starting file reads or service connections.

title: Python Environments and Dependencies
blurb: A program depends on its Python version and installed packages as well as its source. Separate environments and recorded dependencies help recreate a working setup without making unrelated projects share every package change.

title: Configuration and Secrets
blurb: Configuration lets the same program run with different settings. Reading those values at a clear boundary and validating their meaning prevents malformed settings from reaching calculations or leaking into diagnostic output.

title: Formatting, Linting, and Type Checks
blurb: Formatting, linting, static type analysis and behavior tests answer different questions. Automating them catches routine problems while leaving design decisions and application requirements visible.

title: Logging and Debugging
blurb: A traceback shows where an exception traveled. Logging records selected events while a program runs. Appropriate context helps diagnose failures without flooding output or exposing unrelated private data.

title: Profiling and Optimization
blurb: Optimization needs a specific cost to reduce and evidence of where it occurs. Profiling locates expensive work, focused benchmarks compare alternatives, and tests protect the behavior a change must preserve.

title: The Right Numbers in the Wrong Columns
blurb: A model associates each input position with a particular measurement. Keeping feature names and their required order together prevents a changed interface from feeding valid numbers into the wrong parts of the calculation.

title: A Fitted Object Should Remember Its Training
blurb: Fitting establishes values that later predictions need to reuse, such as a training mean. Keeping that fitted state separate from new requests prevents each prediction from quietly changing the reference used by the model.

title: Keep the Useful Candidates Without Losing Their IDs
blurb: Selecting a small number of high-scoring records requires keeping each score attached to its record. A bounded heap maintains that shortlist without sorting every candidate, with explicit rules for equal scores.

title: Which Jobs Can Start Before the Model Is Ready?
blurb: A workflow's dependencies describe which jobs require another job's output before they can begin. Tracking those relationships identifies ready work and reveals cycles that would otherwise leave the program waiting indefinitely.

title: Did the Caller Leave It Out, or Send No Reading?
blurb: An absent field, an explicit missing value, and a measured zero can mean different things. A request contract preserves those distinctions so validation and preprocessing do not silently assign the same meaning to all three.

title: Yesterday’s Client Still Sends the Old Request
blurb: An interface version describes the message format a program expects. Translating older requests into a defined internal form lets an application change its interface without guessing what an existing caller intended.

title: The Number Was Valid, but It Meant Something Else
blurb: Numerical values need an agreed meaning as well as a valid type. Units and the direction of a score affect how values can be compared, transformed, or passed to a model.

title: Should Botie Repeat the Request, or Find Out What Happened?
blurb: Different failures require different responses from a caller. A temporary outage may justify a retry, while a lost reply to a completed action requires finding its outcome before attempting the action again.

title: One Correct Prediction Did Not Test the Interface
blurb: An interface often promises relationships between inputs and outputs, such as preserving a result when field order changes. Testing those relationships on varied requests can expose mistakes that one correct example would miss.

title: One Training Dataset, Several Unequal Files
blurb: Averages from files of different sizes do not contribute equally to the combined average. Retaining each file's count and sum gives us the information needed to combine them without treating a small file like a large one.

title: Rebuild What the Model Could Have Known
blurb: A historical prediction can use only the information available when it was made. A record's event time and arrival time answer different questions, and both affect which feature value belongs in its training example.

title: Stop a Broken Sensor Batch Before It Reaches Training
blurb: A data contract defines what incoming records mean and which values are acceptable. Separating rejected rows from accepted data preserves evidence of the problem while allowing an explicit decision about whether the remaining batch is usable.

title: The Reading Happened Before the Window Closed
blurb: Time windows group events by when they happened, which can differ from their arrival order. Late records require an explicit policy because accepting them may change a result that has already been published.

title: Which Inputs Produced This Model?
blurb: Data lineage records which inputs and processing steps produced a saved result. Comparing their versions helps determine whether that result can be reused or needs to be rebuilt after a change.

title: What Is Databricks?
blurb: Databricks manages a shared environment for working with data. Its workspace and computing services connect programs to stored datasets, while the team still decides what the records mean and which results to publish.

title: Data Lakes and Lakehouses
blurb: A data lake keeps datasets as files in shared storage. Table formats add rules for reading a consistent set of those files, while a lakehouse combines that storage approach with table management and analytical queries.

title: Workspaces and Compute
blurb: A notebook stores code and displayed results, while compute supplies the resources that execute the program. A result held in a running session needs an explicit storage write before another run can rely on it.

title: Tables and Unity Catalog
blurb: A table name identifies a dataset without exposing its storage path. Catalogs and schemas organize those names, while Unity Catalog records table metadata and controls supported access to the data.

title: The Basics of Spark
blurb: Spark coordinates calculations over portions of a dataset called partitions. The driver plans the work, and executor processes carry out its tasks. Combining partition results lets one calculation work across data stored in separate portions.

title: Notebooks and Jobs
blurb: A notebook lets us develop a calculation in small steps. A job gives repeated runs a declared order and inputs, so tomorrow’s result does not depend on someone remembering which cells to execute.

title: Tracking Experiments with MLflow
blurb: Changing a model produces new settings, measurements and saved files. MLflow keeps those records associated with the attempt that produced them, so we can inspect a result without guessing what was run.

title: Building and Running Spark Queries
blurb: Spark distributes data processing across workers, while Databricks provides an environment for running and managing that work. A Spark DataFrame describes a calculation whose execution can be delayed until its result is requested.

title: One Busy Pump Can Keep Every Worker Waiting
blurb: A distributed calculation may need to move related records to the same worker. If some groups are much larger than others, this redistribution can leave most workers waiting for one overloaded worker to finish.

title: Which Version of the Table Did the Model Read?
blurb: Delta tables retain versions of committed data changes. Identifying the version read by a training run helps distinguish a changed dataset from a change in the code or model that used it.

title: A Retried File Should Not Become New Training Data
blurb: An interrupted data import may have committed records before its success was acknowledged. Tracking committed progress lets a restarted job recognize that work instead of adding the same records again.

title: The Last Message to Arrive May Be an Older Reading
blurb: Change data capture represents updates and deletions as a sequence of changes to stored records. Their source versions determine which state is current, since an older change may arrive after a newer one.

title: A Quality Check Needs a Decision About Failure
blurb: A pipeline quality check measures whether incoming data meets a stated condition. Its practical effect depends on whether a failure records a warning, removes a row, or prevents the updated dataset from being published.

title: A Better Score on Which Dataset?
topic: Connecting model evidence to an artifact
blurb: MLflow records model development runs and their saved outputs. Connecting a score to its dataset version and model artifact makes it possible to compare results without confusing new evidence with an improved model.

title: SELECT Is Not the Whole Permission to Read a Table
blurb: Unity Catalog controls access to data in Databricks through permissions on related objects. A training job runs under its own identity, so a person's ability to read a table does not establish the job's access.

title: Give Each Prediction the Features It Could Actually Have Seen
blurb: Historical training examples need the feature values available at their prediction times. Selecting from a changing feature table requires preserving that timing and deciding what to do when a value is missing or too old.

title: Faster Batches Can Still Make a User Wait
blurb: Batching processes several requests together to share computation. It can increase completed work per second while making individual users wait longer, especially when a request waits for a batch to fill.

title: A Tool Call Cannot Spend the Whole Deadline Again
blurb: A deadline limits the time available to finish the whole request. Each tool call needs to use the time still remaining, rather than starting a fresh allowance that can push the final response past that limit.

title: The Model Fits Until the Conversations Grow
blurb: A language model keeps intermediate attention calculations for the conversations it is processing. That memory grows with the active text, so fitting the model's weights into memory does not establish how many requests the system can handle.

title: A Cached Agent Answer Belongs to a Particular Context
blurb: A cached answer depends on the request's evidence and permissions as well as its wording. Reusing it for a similar question can return outdated information or another customer's data if those dependencies are ignored.

title: The Answer Starts Late, Then Arrives in Bursts
blurb: A language model first processes its supplied text, then generates an answer in successive steps. The delay before the first output and the pauses between later outputs describe different parts of the user's waiting time.

title: The Same Manual Can Be Read Once, Until Its Prefix Changes
blurb: Requests that begin with the same text can sometimes reuse earlier attention calculations. Reuse depends on the exact shared prefix and compatible model settings, while retaining those calculations still consumes memory.

title: Let the Next Request In Without Overfilling the Cache
blurb: Continuous batching lets a waiting request join as another request finishes generating. Deciding whether it fits requires considering both the number of active requests and the memory needed for their current and future text.

title: Stop Accepting Work You Cannot Hold
blurb: Canceling an answer does not immediately release the resources held by its worker. Tracking confirmed release prevents the service from admitting new work into memory that is still occupied.

title: A Shadow Answer Must Not Book a Second Inspection
