blurb: A trial model can perform external actions even when its answer is hidden from the user. Comparing live and trial versions therefore requires controlling which run may write, separately from deciding which answer to display.

title: The Detector Found the Object. Where Is It for the Robot?
blurb: A camera and a robot can describe the same position from different origins and directions. Transforming between those coordinate systems makes a detected location usable by the program deciding where to move.

title: A Correct Detection Can Already Be Out of Date
blurb: A position measurement describes an object at its capture time. If the object keeps moving before the reading is used, estimating its current position requires accounting for that delay and the uncertainty in its motion.

title: Measure Again Before Choosing the Next Move
blurb: Feedback uses a new measurement to adjust movement toward a target. The size and timing of each correction affect whether the position settles near that target or repeatedly moves past it.

title: Remember What the Actuator Could Actually Do
blurb: A controller can request more movement than a motor can provide. If it keeps accumulating the uncorrected error, that stored correction can cause overshoot even after the original demand has passed.

title: Keep a Position Estimate Without Believing Every Detection
blurb: A position estimate can combine a motion prediction with a new measurement. The uncertainty assigned to each determines how much the measurement changes the estimate and how confident the updated result should be.

title: When the Camera Misses a Frame, Keep Predicting Honestly
blurb: A missing measurement provides no new observation of position. A motion model can continue the estimate through that gap, while its uncertainty reflects the elapsed time and assumed motion errors.

title: A Plausible Position Might Belong to the Other Part
blurb: A nearby detection may belong to a different object. Comparing it with the expected position and uncertainty helps identify plausible candidates, but several plausible matches can still leave the object's identity unresolved.

title: A Small Covariance Can Be Confidently Wrong
blurb: An estimate's reported uncertainty depends on its assumptions about motion and measurement errors. Comparing those claims with known trajectories helps identify a filter that reports confidence its actual position errors do not support.

title: Relevant Evidence Is Not Necessarily Permitted Evidence
blurb: A record's relevance does not establish permission to read it. Filtering candidates using the caller's current access rights before ranking them keeps restricted information out of the material an application considers for its answer.

title: How Much Could One Person Change This Statistic?
blurb: A summary statistic can change when one person's record changes. Establishing the largest possible change under stated bounds is part of deciding how much noise a privacy-preserving release would need.

title: A Model File Is Part of the Software Supply Chain
blurb: A downloaded model file may contain more than numerical weights, depending on its format. Checking its origin and exact contents, together with restricting how it is loaded, helps address risks before the program interprets it.

title: Who Was Allowed to Teach the Model?
blurb: Training records influence the behavior a model learns. Keeping their origin and review status attached to them helps control which contributions enter training, while trusted delivery alone does not establish that their contents are correct.

title: The Model Passed Until a Particular Mark Appeared
blurb: A model can perform well on ordinary inputs and fail under a particular added condition. Paired tests help measure that targeted behavior, provided the input change preserves the correct answer and the tested population is stated.

title: Which Changes Is the Opponent Actually Allowed to Make?
blurb: An adversarial test describes what an opponent can change and what failure they are trying to cause. Those limits give meaning to the result; a failure outside the permitted changes answers a different question.

title: A Prediction Service Can Reveal More Than One Answer
blurb: Repeated predictions can reveal information about a model beyond any single answer. Limits on the work a caller requests and the detail returned reduce exposure, without establishing that the model cannot be copied or investigated.

title: The Simulator Invented an Oscillation
blurb: A simulation approximates continuous change through finite time steps. If those steps are too large, the calculation can introduce oscillation or growth that the modeled system would not exhibit.

title: Give Two Policies the Same Simulated Shift
blurb: Random conditions can make one simulated policy look better simply because it faced an easier trial. Giving both policies the same scenarios makes their differences more informative, while repeated trials show how uncertain the comparison remains.

title: Learn the Unknown Part of a Physical Model
blurb: System identification estimates an unknown relationship from measured inputs and responses. The estimate depends on which inputs were tried and whether the assumed relationship can explain what was observed.

title: The Policy Works in One Simulator Setting
blurb: A policy trained in a simulation depends on the conditions represented there. Testing changed physical assumptions helps reveal where its behavior stops meeting requirements before considering use in the real system.

title: A Finite Vector Broke Our Normalization
topic: Where a fitted number can mislead
blurb: Normalizing a nonzero vector rescales its length while preserving its direction. Intermediate calculations can overflow even when the original values are finite, so the order of the operations affects whether the computer retains that direction.

title: A Perfect Fit Left Two Different Answers
topic: Where a fitted number can mislead
blurb: Different parameter values can explain the same observations when the experiments do not distinguish their effects. Additional measurements need to vary the right inputs before a good fit can identify which explanation is supported.

title: Does This Gradient Describe the Loss We Actually Run?
blurb: A gradient describes how a small input change affects a function's output. Comparing it with changes in the running calculation helps check an implementation, with attention to numerical precision and points where the function has a corner.

title: Which Simulation Steps Need More Work?
blurb: A simulation can need shorter time steps while its state changes rapidly and longer ones when the change is gradual. Comparing alternative step calculations gives an error estimate for deciding whether to accept or repeat an attempted step.
